title: Spiral Matrix
description: Brute force to optimized: a visited matrix simulation versus four shrinking boundaries.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an m by n matrix, return all of its elements visited in spiral order, starting from the top left corner, moving right across the top, down the right side, left across the bottom, and up the left side, spiraling inward until every element has been visited.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given an m by n matrix, return all of its elements visited in spiral order, starting from the top left corner, moving right across the top, down the right side, left across the bottom, and up the left side, spiraling inward until every element has been visited.

blocks.title: Analogy: Peeling an Onion Ring by Ring
blocks.text: Like peeling a rectangular onion one full outer ring at a time: walk all the way around the outermost layer, then move one layer inward and repeat, until nothing is left in the center.

blocks.caption: Walk the outer ring first, then spiral inward one ring at a time

blocks.text: Edge case: a single row [[1, 2, 3, 4]]
With only one row, the spiral is simply that row read left to right, since there is no room to turn downward at all: [1, 2, 3, 4].
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask what information a direct simulation is really tracking, and whether all of it is actually necessary.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A direct simulation, walk in the current direction and turn when blocked, works, but it needs a full visited matrix just to detect when a cell has already been used, duplicating information the shrinking shape of the walk already implies.

Observation 2: Rotate Array and Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array already showed that a range which shrinks predictably from both ends can replace an explicit step by step simulation entirely.

Observation 3: Here, the unvisited region is always a rectangle, described completely by four boundaries, top, bottom, left, and right, that shrink inward by exactly one after each side is walked, with no need to check individual cells for having been visited before.

Observation 4: The one subtlety is that after walking the top row and right column, the bottom row or left column may no longer exist, for instance on a single remaining row, so a guard check before walking each of those last two sides is required, confirmed by tracing the 3 by 3 example through to its correct spiral order.
Recognizing that the unvisited region is always a shrinking rectangle, fully described by just four boundary values, is what replaces an entire visited matrix with a handful of integers.
6. Brute Force Solution
Simulate the walk directly using a visited matrix: move in the current direction, and whenever the next cell would go out of bounds or has already been visited, turn 90 degrees clockwise instead.
Step by step algorithm

items: Keep a visited matrix the same size as the input, all initially false.
Start at the top left cell moving right, and mark each visited cell as true while recording its value.
Whenever the next cell in the current direction is out of bounds or already visited, rotate the direction clockwise (right becomes down, down becomes left, left becomes up, up becomes right).
Stop once every cell has been visited.

codes.python:
def spiral_order(matrix):
    rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    visited = [[False] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
    directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]           # right, down, left, up
    result = []
    r, c, d = 0, 0, 0
    for _ in range(rows * cols):
        result.append(matrix[r][c])
        visited[r][c] = True
        nr, nc = r + directions[d][0], c + directions[d][1]
        if not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols) or visited[nr][nc]:
            d = (d + 1) % 4                                        # turn clockwise when blocked
            nr, nc = r + directions[d][0], c + directions[d][1]
        r, c = nr, nc
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]
    print(spiral_order(matrix))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The four possible directions are stored as row and column offsets in a fixed clockwise order, so turning is just advancing to the next entry in that list.
The visited matrix is checked before every move to decide whether the current direction is still valid or whether a turn is needed.
The loop runs for exactly rows times cols steps, guaranteeing every cell is visited exactly once regardless of the matrix's shape.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
The direction only turns when genuinely blocked, so this correctly traces the spiral and visits every cell exactly once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m times n), visiting every cell once.
Space: O(m times n), for the visited matrix.

Limitation: a full visited matrix is unnecessary bookkeeping. The four edges of the current unvisited region shrink in a predictable pattern that can be tracked directly with just four boundary variables.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: an entire visited matrix is kept alive just to answer "has this cell already been used", when the shrinking rectangle shape of the walk already answers that question implicitly.

What tracking four boundaries fixes directly: top, bottom, left, and right describe the entire unvisited region at any moment, and walking each of the four sides in order, then shrinking the boundary just used, replaces per-cell visited checks entirely.

What has to be guarded carefully: after the top row and right column are walked, the bottom row or left column may no longer exist as a distinct side, so each of those last two sides needs an explicit check before being walked.

The core idea: repeatedly walk the top row, right column, bottom row (if it still exists), and left column (if it still exists), shrinking each boundary inward by one after its side is walked, until the boundaries cross.

Track four boundaries: the topmost row, bottommost row, leftmost column, and rightmost column still unvisited. Walk across the top row, down the right column, across the bottom row (if it still exists), and up the left column (if it still exists), then shrink each boundary inward by one after its side is walked, repeating until the boundaries cross.
9. Optimized Solution
Walk the four sides of the current boundary rectangle in order, shrinking the boundaries after each side.

blocks.caption: Optimized: walk the four current boundaries directly, shrinking them after each side

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because at every point in the walk, the unvisited cells always form a perfect rectangle described exactly by the current top, bottom, left, and right boundaries, so walking each of its four sides once and then shrinking the corresponding boundary correctly peels off exactly one ring without ever revisiting or skipping a cell.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m times n), matching the output size exactly, visiting every cell once.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the output, since only four boundary variables are kept.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Since the output itself must contain every one of the m times n cells, O(m times n) time is already optimal, and the four boundary variables replace an entire visited matrix with a handful of integers, the real improvement this problem offers over the brute force.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting the guard checks (top less than or equal to bottom, left less than or equal to right) before walking the bottom row and left column, which can otherwise re-visit or skip cells in matrices with only one remaining row or column.
Mixing up which boundary shrinks after which side is walked.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Draw the shrinking rectangle of boundaries on a small grid before writing any code. It makes the four guard conditions and the order of shrinking obvious rather than something to memorize.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the extra visited matrix", think: four shrinking boundaries, top, bottom, left, right, describe the unvisited region directly.
If the interviewer says "what about a single row or column", think: guard checks before the bottom row and left column prevent revisiting or skipping cells.
If the interviewer says "can you fill a matrix in spiral order instead of reading one", think: the exact same four shrinking boundaries, but writing increasing values into each cell instead of reading them out.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why do the bottom row and left column each need an extra guard check before being walked, but the top row and right column do not?
How would you adapt this approach to generate a spiral matrix filled with 1 through n squared instead of reading an existing one?
How would the boundaries change if the spiral needed to move counter-clockwise instead?
What is the exact number of rings a matrix with m rows and n columns has?
How would you return the spiral order of only a rectangular sub-region of a larger matrix?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Rotate Array, whose in place reversal trick replaces a step by step simulation with a fixed, predictable sequence of operations, the same instinct applied here to boundaries instead of reversals.
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array, whose shrinking left and right range is the one dimensional ancestor of the four shrinking boundaries used here in two dimensions.

Any matrix traversal problem describing a specific visiting order (diagonal, zigzag, boustrophedon), where identifying the shrinking or shifting boundary of the unvisited region is usually the key insight.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(m times n) time, O(m times n) space for the visited matrix. Optimized: O(m times n) time, O(1) extra space using four shrinking boundaries.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: four shrinking boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) walked in order, replacing an explicit visited matrix simulation.

Core Idea: the unvisited region is always a rectangle fully described by four boundary values, so walking each of its four sides in order and shrinking the boundary just used peels off exactly one ring at a time.
Time: O(m times n) for both the brute force and the optimized approach.
Space: O(m times n) for the brute force's visited matrix, O(1) extra for the optimized approach's four boundaries.
Most Important Observation: the shape of the unvisited region shrinks predictably, so tracking that shape directly is far cheaper than tracking every individual visited cell.
Interview Difficulty: the four boundary idea is standard; correctly guarding the bottom row and left column against matrices with few remaining rows or columns is where most bugs happen.
One line memory trick: walk top, right, bottom, left, shrinking each boundary after its side, and guard the last two sides.
